Kate and Marcus get married
HUDSON VALLEY, NEW YORK
An old red barn, a flower girl with a strong arm, and a speech
practiced on the dog.
A STORY BY MAYA HARTLEY
Getting ready
Kate has been my sister-in-law for twelve years and my friend
for longer than that, so when she asked me to be the one who
wrote this up, I said yes before she had finished the sentence.
Here it is, Kate. You can fix my spelling later.
They got married on a Saturday in May at an old red barn in the
Hudson Valley, with an orchard on one side and a field of long
grass on the other. The morning was all hairpins and coffee. Ivy
had been made official flower girl and took the job very
seriously, which mostly meant sitting very still in her flower
crown and watching every single pin go in.
Hairpins, coffee and one very serious flower girl.
The aisle
The aisle was mown into the grass that morning, between rows
of borrowed chairs. Ivy went first, scattering petals in perfectly
even handfuls, as practiced, and then forgot the plan halfway
and threw the whole basket at Grandpa Joe. Everyone turned
round to watch. Nobody minded.
Ivy, moments before she threw the whole basket at Grandpa Joe.
The vows
They wrote their own. Marcus promised to always let Kate have
the window seat. Kate promised to learn which way round the
dishwasher goes. Then they both got serious for about a minute,
under an arch of white flowers that Ruth had spent three days
building, and there was not a dry eye in the field. Finn, fourteen
and very grown up in a borrowed suit, handed over the rings
without dropping either one, and then looked enormously
relieved.
Under the arch Ruth spent three days building.
Then they walked back down the aisle through a storm of
petals, and the whole family lined up in front of the barn for the
one photo where everybody is looking the same way.
Everyone, looking the same way, just this once.
The speeches
Tom gave the brother-of-the-bride speech. He had practiced it
on me nine times and on the dog twice. It had a story about Kate
driving the family car into a mailbox when she was seventeen,
which she has never admitted, and a list of all the boyfriends
Tom had not approved of before Marcus, which was long. Kate
laughed so hard she had to cover her face.
Tom gets to the part about the mailbox.
Marcus filmed his own wedding speeches, of course. Here is the
bit everyone has asked for.
The dancing
Grandpa Joe is seventy this year and is still the best dancer in
any room. He danced with every single person there, oldest to
youngest, and finished with Ivy, who stood on his shoes for the
whole song.
Grandpa Joe and his best dance partner.
The band played until midnight. Ruth and her sister took over
the floor for one song and would not give it back. Finn, who had
sworn he would not dance under any circumstances, was
spotted dancing under several circumstances. Biscuit, who was
not invited, appeared at nine o’clock having escaped from the
car, and was allowed to stay on the condition that he did not eat
the cake. He ate some of the cake.
At the end of the night we all lined the path with sparklers and
Kate and Marcus ran through the middle, laughing, out to the
car and off to Italy. Leo, who was supposed to be asleep, waved
his sparkler like a lightsaber the whole time.
Congratulations, you two. We love you.
Off to Italy.
Down the aisle and out through the petals. Mr. and Mrs., at last.
